why: SQL is the most requested skill across data, BA and support roles. Interviews almost always include a live query exercise.
outcome: write SELECT queries with filters, joins, aggregations, CTEs and window functions, and explain what they return.

lessons.title: Read data: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY
text: A table is a set of rows with named columns. SELECT chooses columns, FROM chooses the table, WHERE keeps only the rows that match a condition, ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT keeps the first rows.
SQL is written in that order but executed in another one: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. This explains why you cannot use a column alias in WHERE.
points: Text values use single quotes: 'Paris'.
NULL means unknown: test it with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never = NULL.
Combine conditions with AND / OR and use parentheses to be explicit.
IN ('a','b') and BETWEEN 10 AND 20 keep queries short; LIKE 'Data%' matches a prefix.

example.code:
SELECT first_name, city, salary
FROM employees
WHERE city IN ('Paris', 'Lyon')
  AND salary >= 40000
  AND manager_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 10;
example.note: Top 10 salaries in Paris or Lyon, among people who have a manager.

lessons.title: Summarise: GROUP BY, aggregates, HAVING
text: Aggregate functions turn many rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. With GROUP BY you get one result row per group.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after the aggregate is computed.
points: Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) ignores NULLs; COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts unique values.
Use ROUND(AVG(x), 2) to present clean numbers.

example.code:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount, ROUND(AVG(salary), 0) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE hired_on >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;
example.note: Departments with at least 5 people hired since 2023, by average salary.

lessons.title: Combine tables: JOINs
text: A JOIN matches rows of two tables on a condition, usually a foreign key equal to a primary key (orders.customer_id = customers.id).
INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows. LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side with NULL when nothing matches; that is how you find what is missing.
points: Always alias tables (o, c) and prefix columns: o.amount, c.name.
Check row counts before and after a join: a join on a non-unique key multiplies rows.
LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL finds rows with no match (customers without orders).

example.code:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
example.note: Customers without orders still appear, with 0 orders and 0 revenue.

lessons.title: Go further: CTEs and window functions
text: A CTE (WITH name AS (...)) names an intermediate result so a long query reads top to bottom.
Window functions compute a value per row while looking at other rows, without collapsing them: rankings, running totals, the previous value. They are the classic intermediate interview question.
points: ROW_NUMBER() gives 1, 2, 3; RANK() leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK() does not.
PARTITION BY restarts the calculation for each group; ORDER BY inside OVER sets the order.
LAG(x) / LEAD(x) read the previous / next row: perfect for month-over-month changes.
SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY day) gives a running total.

example.code:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', ordered_at) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change_vs_prev
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
example.note: DATE_TRUNC is PostgreSQL / Snowflake / BigQuery-style; SQL Server uses DATETRUNC or FORMAT.

lessons.title: Performance: indexes and query plans
text: A query that takes seconds on a big table usually reads every row. An index is a sorted copy of one or more columns with pointers to the rows, like the index of a book: the database jumps to the right rows instead of scanning everything.

EXPLAIN shows the plan the database chose; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows real timings. Look for full scans (Seq Scan) on large tables, row estimates far from reality and sorts or joins that spill to disk.
points: Index the columns you filter and join on most; put the most selective, equality-filtered column first.
Functions on a column (WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026) prevent using its index: filter on a range instead.
Every index speeds up reads but slows down writes and takes space: do not index everything.
Select only the columns you need instead of SELECT * on wide tables.

example.note: Measure before and after: the plan, not intuition, tells you what changed.

lessons.title: Subqueries, CTEs and recursive CTEs
text: A subquery is a query inside another one. It can return a single value (a scalar subquery in SELECT or WHERE), a list (WHERE id IN (SELECT ...)) or a whole table (FROM (SELECT ...) AS t). A correlated subquery refers to the outer row, for example the average salary of the current employee's department: conceptually it is evaluated once per outer row, which can be slow on large tables if the optimizer cannot rewrite it as a join.

A CTE does the same job but gives the intermediate result a name, so multi-step logic reads from top to bottom and the same step can be referenced twice. Since PostgreSQL 12, a CTE used once is usually inlined like a subquery, so it is not slower; WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (...) forces it to be computed once. Choose by readability: a short filter fits in a subquery, three or more steps belong in CTEs.

EXISTS and NOT EXISTS check whether at least one matching row exists and stop at the first match. Prefer NOT EXISTS to NOT IN: if the subquery returns a single NULL, x NOT IN (...) is never true and the query silently returns nothing.

A recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) walks hierarchies such as org charts, category trees or bills of materials. An anchor query returns the starting rows, then a recursive part joins back to the CTE and adds rows until a step returns nothing new. SQL Server writes the same query without the RECURSIVE keyword; Oracle also offers CONNECT BY.
points: A scalar subquery must return at most one row, otherwise the query fails.
Give every derived table an alias: FROM (SELECT ...) AS t (required by most databases).
Use NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN when the subquery column can be NULL.
Use UNION ALL in a recursive CTE and add a depth limit to stop on cyclic data.
Recursive CTEs can also generate rows (a list of dates), but PostgreSQL's generate_series is simpler for that.

example.code:
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, first_name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM employees
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL              -- anchor: the top of the org chart
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.first_name, e.manager_id, c.depth + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id   -- recursive step: direct reports
  WHERE c.depth < 10                    -- safety stop
)
SELECT depth, first_name
FROM chain
ORDER BY depth, first_name;
example.note: Each level of the org chart is added until no new employee is found.

lessons.title: Window functions in depth: frames, running totals and ties
text: OVER has three parts: PARTITION BY (which rows belong together), ORDER BY (in which order) and the frame (which rows around the current one are used). Ranking functions and LAG / LEAD only use the first two; aggregates such as SUM or AVG over a window also use the frame.

The default frame is a classic trap. With ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the database uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. RANGE treats rows with the same ORDER BY value as peers, so two orders on the same day get the same running total. Write ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a strict row-by-row total, and ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a 7-row moving average.

Decide explicitly how to handle ties. ROW_NUMBER picks an arbitrary order among ties unless ORDER BY ends with a unique column (ORDER BY amount DESC, id). For a top 3 per group that keeps ties, filter on DENSE_RANK() <= 3. NTILE(4) splits rows into quartiles. FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE return the edges of the frame, which is why LAST_VALUE with the default frame returns the current row.

Window functions are computed after WHERE, so you cannot filter on them directly: compute them in a CTE and filter outside. Snowflake, BigQuery and Databricks add QUALIFY for this; PostgreSQL does not.
points: LAG(x, 1, 0) takes an offset and a default for the first row.
SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g) without ORDER BY gives the group total: x / that total is a share.
WINDOW w AS (...) names a window definition you can reuse (PostgreSQL, MySQL 8).
A 7-row average is a 7-day average only if every day has a row: fill gaps first.

example.code:
SELECT store_id, order_day, revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER w_running AS running_total,
       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY order_day
             ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg_7_rows,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY order_day) AS change_vs_prev
FROM daily_sales
WINDOW w_running AS (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY order_day
                     ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
ORDER BY store_id, order_day;
example.note: daily_sales has one row per store and day; revenue is numeric.

lessons.title: NULLs, three-valued logic and data cleaning
text: In SQL a condition is TRUE, FALSE or UNKNOWN. Any comparison with NULL (NULL = NULL, status <> 'cancelled' when status is NULL) is UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. So WHERE status <> 'cancelled' silently drops the rows where status is NULL, and NOT (UNKNOWN) is still UNKNOWN. Aggregates skip NULLs, except COUNT(*): AVG(bonus) averages only the people who have a bonus.

A few functions make NULLs explicit. COALESCE(a, b, c) returns the first non-NULL value. NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a equals b, the standard way to avoid a division by zero: revenue / NULLIF(visits, 0). a IS DISTINCT FROM b compares values while treating two NULLs as equal. In PostgreSQL, NULLs sort last in ascending order and first in descending order; NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST makes it explicit (MySQL and SQL Server do not support this syntax).

Data cleaning in SQL relies on the same small toolbox: CASE WHEN to map messy values to clean categories, TRIM, LOWER, REPLACE and SPLIT_PART to normalise text, CAST(x AS DATE) or x::date to convert types, DATE_TRUNC, EXTRACT and intervals (created_at + INTERVAL '7 days') for dates. One value that cannot be cast makes the whole query fail, so filter or fix bad values first (SQL Server has TRY_CAST, PostgreSQL does not).
Keep the raw table untouched and put cleaning rules in a view or a new table: you can rerun them, explain every rule and compare before and after.
points: WHERE status <> 'x' OR status IS NULL keeps NULL rows on purpose.
NULL in arithmetic or || concatenation makes the result NULL; CONCAT() skips NULLs.
COUNT(*) - COUNT(col) is the number of NULLs in col.
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE col IS NULL) is a PostgreSQL shortcut for SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).

example.code:
CREATE VIEW customers_clean AS
SELECT
  id,
  INITCAP(TRIM(city)) AS city,
  LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS email,
  CASE
    WHEN LOWER(TRIM(status)) IN ('active', 'actif') THEN 'active'
    WHEN status IS NULL OR TRIM(status) = '' THEN 'unknown'
    ELSE 'inactive'
  END AS status,
  COALESCE(phone, 'n/a') AS phone,
  ROUND(revenue::numeric / NULLIF(orders, 0), 2) AS avg_basket,
  signup_at::date AS signup_day
FROM raw_customers;
example.note: INITCAP and the :: cast are PostgreSQL; elsewhere use CAST(x AS DATE) and your database's text functions.

lessons.title: Transactions and isolation basics
text: A transaction groups statements that must succeed or fail together: BEGIN, the statements, then COMMIT to keep the changes or ROLLBACK to cancel them. This is the A of ACID (atomicity): a money transfer must never debit one account without crediting the other. In PostgreSQL a statement outside BEGIN runs in its own transaction and is committed immediately (autocommit). Check your SQL client's setting: some tools open a transaction for you and keep locks until you commit.

Isolation controls what a transaction sees of the others running at the same time. The standard levels are READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE; each one prevents more anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom rows). READ COMMITTED is the default in PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle, REPEATABLE READ in MySQL InnoDB. PostgreSQL never shows uncommitted data, even in READ UNCOMMITTED. Under SERIALIZABLE, PostgreSQL may abort a transaction with a serialization failure that the application must retry.

Writes lock the rows they change until the transaction ends. A long transaction blocks other writers and, in PostgreSQL, prevents old row versions from being cleaned up. Keep transactions short and never wait for user input inside one. To avoid a lost update (two sessions read the same value, both write), update in a single statement (SET stock = stock - 1) or lock the rows first with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
points: In PostgreSQL an error inside a transaction aborts it: every next statement fails until ROLLBACK.
SAVEPOINT s and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s undo part of a transaction.
DDL is transactional in PostgreSQL (a CREATE TABLE can be rolled back), not in MySQL or Oracle.
Check how many rows each UPDATE touched before you COMMIT.

example.note: Other sessions see either all three changes or none of them.

lessons.title: Change data safely: INSERT ... SELECT, UPDATE with joins, upserts
text: Writing data is where SQL mistakes become expensive. Before any UPDATE or DELETE, run the same WHERE clause as a SELECT COUNT(*) and check the number. Work inside a transaction so you can roll back, and in PostgreSQL add RETURNING to see the rows you changed (SQL Server uses OUTPUT). An UPDATE without WHERE changes every row of the table.

INSERT INTO target (cols) SELECT ... copies the result of a query; always list the columns so a new column or a different order cannot shift values. To update from another table, PostgreSQL writes UPDATE t SET ... FROM s WHERE t.id = s.id, SQL Server UPDATE t SET ... FROM t JOIN s ON ..., MySQL UPDATE t JOIN s ON ... SET .... If the source has several rows per target row, the result is unpredictable: deduplicate the source first. PostgreSQL deletes with a join using DELETE FROM t USING s WHERE ....

An upsert inserts new rows and updates existing ones. PostgreSQL uses INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col, which needs a unique constraint or index on the key; MySQL has INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE. The standard MERGE INTO target USING source ON ... WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT exists in PostgreSQL 15+, SQL Server, Oracle, Snowflake and BigQuery. Upserts make loads idempotent: rerunning the same load does not create duplicates.
points: Run the WHERE as a SELECT first, then the UPDATE or DELETE inside BEGIN.
Delete or update millions of rows in batches to keep locks and logs small.
TRUNCATE empties a whole table instantly: it is never a replacement for DELETE ... WHERE.
A load that can safely run twice is worth more than a fast one that cannot.

example.code:
-- Load staging rows into customers; safe to run again
BEGIN;

INSERT INTO customers (id, email, city, updated_at)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (id) id, LOWER(TRIM(email)), city, loaded_at
FROM staging_customers
ORDER BY id, loaded_at DESC
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE
SET email = EXCLUDED.email,
    city = EXCLUDED.city,
    updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
WHERE customers.updated_at < EXCLUDED.updated_at
RETURNING id;

COMMIT;
example.note: DISTINCT ON (PostgreSQL) keeps the latest staging row per id: without it, two rows with the same id make ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE fail.

lessons.title: Cohorts, retention and funnels in SQL
text: Data Analyst live tests and take-home cases come back to the same three questions: do the customers we acquire come back (cohorts and retention), how many buy more than once (repeat purchase), and where do visitors drop out before buying (funnel). None needs an exotic function: a CTE, MIN(), a date truncated to the month, COUNT(DISTINCT ...) and CASE inside an aggregate are enough. What the interviewer really checks is whether you define the metric before writing the query, and whether your numbers survive a sanity check.

A cohort is a group of users who share a starting event in the same period. Two definitions are common: the signup cohort (month of customers.created_at) and the first-order cohort (month of MIN(ordered_at) per customer). They answer different questions, so say which one you use. Build it in two steps: a CTE with one row per customer and their cohort date, then a join back to the activity. In PostgreSQL, DATE_TRUNC('month', ts) gives the month; in SQLite strftime('%Y-%m', ts); in BigQuery DATE_TRUNC(d, MONTH); in SQL Server DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(d), MONTH(d), 1).

Retention by cohort is a table with one row per cohort and one column per month offset: offset 0 is the cohort month itself, offset 1 the next month, and so on. The offset is (year of activity − year of cohort) × 12 + (month of activity − month of cohort). The pivot is conditional aggregation: COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_offset = 1 THEN customer_id END) counts each customer once, and CASE without ELSE returns NULL, which COUNT ignores. Divide by the cohort size, multiplied by 100.0, to get a percentage. State whether retention means 'ordered in that month' (classic) or 'ordered in that month or later' (unbounded): the second is always higher.

The repeat-purchase rate is the share of buyers with at least two orders: aggregate orders per customer first, then count customers with SUM(CASE WHEN orders >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) and divide by the number of buyers, not by all registered customers. A funnel follows the same pattern on event data: one COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event = '...' THEN user_id END) per step (with GA4-style names such as view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase), then the conversion of each step from the previous one and the overall rate from the first step. That is an open funnel; a strict funnel only counts a step when the previous one happened before it, usually within a time window, which needs MIN(at) per user and step.

Most wrong answers come from four pitfalls. Duplicates: a join with orders or a repeated event multiplies rows, so COUNT(*) counts rows, not people; count DISTINCT ids. The incomplete last month: if the data stops on the 13th, the last month looks like a collapse, so exclude it or label it as partial, and leave offsets not yet reached for the newest cohorts empty rather than 0. Time zones: timestamps are often stored in UTC, and an order at 23:30 UTC on 31 January was placed on 1 February in Paris; convert before truncating (PostgreSQL: ts AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Paris' on a timestamptz). Finally, small cohorts: a cohort of 3 customers gives 33% steps, so show the cohort size next to every rate.
points: Define the cohort (signup or first order) and the retention rule before writing SQL.
One row per user and cohort date in a CTE, then join back to the activity.
COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ... THEN user_id END) pivots and counts people, not rows.
Flag the incomplete last month and leave unreached offsets empty, not 0.
Convert UTC timestamps to the business time zone before truncating to day or month.

example.code:
WITH first_orders AS (
  SELECT customer_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(ordered_at)) AS cohort
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
),
activity AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT f.cohort, o.customer_id,
         (EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.ordered_at) - EXTRACT(YEAR FROM f.cohort)) * 12
         + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM o.ordered_at) - EXTRACT(MONTH FROM f.cohort) AS month_offset
  FROM orders o
  JOIN first_orders f ON f.customer_id = o.customer_id
)
SELECT cohort,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_offset = 1 THEN customer_id END)
             / COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id), 1) AS m1_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_offset = 2 THEN customer_id END)
             / COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id), 1) AS m2_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_offset = 3 THEN customer_id END)
             / COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id), 1) AS m3_pct
FROM activity
GROUP BY cohort
ORDER BY cohort;
example.note: PostgreSQL. Retention in % by first-order cohort; DISTINCT in the activity CTE keeps one row per customer and month offset. In SQLite (the practice database) use strftime('%Y-%m', ordered_at) for the month.

items: First n rows (SQL Server: TOP n)
Matches any value in the list
a JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id
All rows of a, NULL when no match
Rows of a with no match in b
CASE WHEN x THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY d)

WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE ...)
Rows with no match, safe with NULLs
WITH RECURSIVE t AS (anchor UNION ALL step)
Walk a hierarchy level by level
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

Lock the rows you are about to update
UPDATE t SET c = s.c FROM s WHERE t.id = s.id
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET c = EXCLUDED.c
MERGE INTO t USING s ON ... WHEN MATCHED THEN ...
Show the rows changed (SQL Server: OUTPUT)
First order per customer: the cohort date
COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k = 1 THEN user_id END)
UTC timestamptz to local time before truncating (PostgreSQL)

pitfalls: Writing = NULL instead of IS NULL: the condition is never true.
Putting a condition on the right table of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE, which silently turns it into an INNER JOIN. Put it in the ON clause instead.
Joining on a key that is not unique and getting duplicated totals.
Using SELECT * in production queries: slower and breaks when columns change.
Using NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL: the query returns no rows at all. Use NOT EXISTS.
Relying on the default window frame for a running total: with RANGE, rows sharing the same ORDER BY value get the same total. Write ROWS BETWEEN ... and add a unique tie-breaker.
Running an UPDATE or DELETE outside a transaction without first checking its WHERE with a SELECT: one typo can change the whole table.

Counting rows instead of people in cohorts and funnels: after a join with orders or with repeated events, COUNT(*) inflates the numbers. Count DISTINCT user ids, and flag a last month that is still incomplete.

exercises.q: List the 5 cities with the most customers, with the number of customers.
exercises.hint: GROUP BY city, ORDER BY the count, LIMIT.
exercises.answer:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY customers DESC
LIMIT 5;

exercises.q: Find customers who never placed an order.
exercises.hint: LEFT JOIN and look for NULL on the orders side.
exercises.answer:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

exercises.q: For each customer, return their most recent order only.
exercises.hint: ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by customer, ordered by date descending.

exercises.q: Rewrite this filter so an index on created_at can be used: WHERE EXTRACT(MONTH FROM created_at) = 1 AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at) = 2026.
exercises.hint: Compare the column itself to a date range.
exercises.answer:
SELECT id, total
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01'
  AND created_at <  '2026-02-01';

exercises.q: List the employees who earn more than the average salary of their own department.
exercises.hint: A correlated subquery that compares with the department of the outer row.
exercises.answer:
SELECT e.first_name, e.department, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
  SELECT AVG(e2.salary)
  FROM employees e2
  WHERE e2.department = e.department
);

exercises.q: Show each order with a running total of amount per customer, strictly row by row even when two orders share a date.
exercises.hint: An explicit ROWS frame and a unique tie-breaker in ORDER BY.
exercises.answer:
SELECT customer_id, ordered_at, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at, id
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, ordered_at, id;

exercises.q: Compute the conversion rate (conversions / clicks, in %) per campaign without failing when a campaign has 0 clicks.
exercises.hint: NULLIF on the divisor, and multiply by 100.0 to avoid integer division.
exercises.answer:
SELECT campaign,
       SUM(clicks) AS clicks,
       SUM(conversions) AS conversions,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(conversions) / NULLIF(SUM(clicks), 0), 1) AS conversion_pct
FROM campaign_stats
GROUP BY campaign;

exercises.q: Load the prices of staging_prices (one row per sku) into products: insert new skus, update the price of existing ones.
exercises.hint: INSERT ... SELECT with ON CONFLICT; products needs a unique constraint on sku.
exercises.answer:
INSERT INTO products (sku, price, updated_at)
SELECT sku, price, NOW()
FROM staging_prices
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
SET price = EXCLUDED.price,
    updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at;

exercises.q: Predict the two numbers this query returns.
exercises.answer: COUNT(*) counts rows (5); COUNT(phone) counts non-NULL values in that column (3). Every aggregate except COUNT(*) ignores NULLs: AVG(phone_bill) divides by the rows that have a value.

exercises.q: Spot the bug: the goal is the cities with more than 10 customers. Which line makes the query fail?
exercises.snippet:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers
WHERE COUNT(*) > 10
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY customers DESC;
exercises.fix:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10
ORDER BY customers DESC;
exercises.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so it cannot use an aggregate. A condition on COUNT(*) goes in HAVING, after GROUP BY. Order of evaluation: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY.

exercises.q: Fix this query (practice database dwh, a small sales data warehouse; dim_customer keeps one row per version of a customer, is_current = 1 for today's). It should give the revenue of registered customers by the city they live in today, but the Lyon and Tunis totals are too high.
exercises.hint: Run it, then count the dim_customer rows per customer_id: how many rows of c does each sale meet?
exercises.answer:
SELECT c.city, ROUND(SUM(f.amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_customer h ON h.customer_key = f.customer_key
JOIN dim_customer c ON c.customer_id = h.customer_id AND c.is_current = 1
GROUP BY c.city;
exercises.start:
SELECT c.city, ROUND(SUM(f.amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_customer h ON h.customer_key = f.customer_key
JOIN dim_customer c ON c.customer_id = h.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city;
exercises.explain: The second join matches every version of the customer, so the sales of customers with history are counted once per version, and in their old city too (fan-out). Keeping only the current version (c.is_current = 1) gives one row per sale. Check any join on a non-unique key: compare COUNT(*) before and after the join.

exercises.q: Fix this query (dwh): the products that sold more than 50 units in Q2. It fails with “misuse of aggregate”.
exercises.hint: WHERE filters rows before grouping; a condition on SUM() belongs after GROUP BY.
exercises.answer:
SELECT p.name, SUM(f.quantity) AS units
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_key = f.product_key
WHERE d.quarter = 2
GROUP BY p.name
HAVING SUM(f.quantity) > 50;
exercises.start:
SELECT p.name, SUM(f.quantity) AS units
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_key = f.product_key
WHERE d.quarter = 2 AND SUM(f.quantity) > 50
GROUP BY p.name;
exercises.explain: WHERE runs before GROUP BY, on single rows: SUM() does not exist yet. Keep the row filter (quarter = 2) in WHERE and move the condition on the total to HAVING. Order of execution: FROM / JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.

exercises.q: Fix this query (dwh): the customers who have not bought anything since 1 May 2025. It returns no rows, although marketing knows some customers stopped buying.
exercises.hint: Some sales have no customer (walk-in sales: customer_key is NULL). What does x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) give?
exercises.answer:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM dim_customer c
WHERE c.is_current = 1
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM fact_sales f
    WHERE f.customer_key = c.customer_key AND f.date_key >= 20250501
  );
exercises.explain: x NOT IN (…, NULL) is never true: x <> NULL is unknown, so every row is filtered out. Use NOT EXISTS (it ignores NULLs), or add WHERE customer_key IS NOT NULL in the subquery. Four customers stopped: C005, C009, C015, C018. (All customer moves happened before May, so the current key is the one used since then.)

exercises.q: Query plan (dwh): there is an index idx_sales_date on fact_sales(date_key), but this query for March reads the whole table (the plan says SCAN). Rewrite the WHERE so SQLite can use the index, keep EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN in front, and run it until the plan says SEARCH … USING INDEX.
exercises.hint: An index on date_key can find a range of date_key values, not values of date_key / 100. date_key looks like 20250315.
exercises.answer:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT SUM(amount)
FROM fact_sales
WHERE date_key >= 20250301 AND date_key < 20250401;
exercises.start:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT SUM(amount)
FROM fact_sales
WHERE date_key / 100 = 202503;
exercises.explain: A calculation or function on the indexed column (date_key / 100, strftime(…, date), LOWER(email), CAST) hides the column from the index: the engine has to compute it for every row. A range on the bare column (>= first day AND < first day of next month, or BETWEEN) is “sargable”: SEARCH … USING INDEX (date_key>? AND date_key<?). Same idea in PostgreSQL, SQL Server or BigQuery partitions: filter the raw column.

exercises.q: Query plan (dwh): looking up one customer's sales scans all of fact_sales. In the same box, create an index named idx_sales_customer on fact_sales(customer_key), then run the EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN below: the plan must use your index.
exercises.hint: CREATE INDEX <name> ON <table> (<column>); then the EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN line. Each run starts from a fresh copy of the database.
exercises.start:
-- 1. Create the index here

-- 2. Then show the plan
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM fact_sales WHERE customer_key = 7;
exercises.explain: SCAN reads every row; SEARCH … USING INDEX idx_sales_customer (customer_key=?) jumps to the matching rows. Index the columns used to filter and join (foreign keys of a fact table are classic candidates), but not everything: each index costs disk space and slows down INSERT / UPDATE. In PostgreSQL the same check is EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) and you look for Seq Scan vs Index Scan.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Data Analyst (1/5). The sales director of a retailer (practice database dwh) writes: “Q2 looks good overall, but is every store growing? Find out what is going on.” Start with the big picture: revenue and number of tickets per quarter.
exercises.hint: Join dim_date for the quarter; count distinct tickets, not lines.
exercises.answer:
SELECT d.quarter, ROUND(SUM(f.amount), 2) AS revenue,
       COUNT(DISTINCT f.ticket_id) AS tickets
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
GROUP BY d.quarter;
exercises.explain: Q1 22,040 (116 tickets) → Q2 27,138 (135 tickets): +23% revenue, +16% tickets, so the average basket grew too. A good first step in any case: one line that sizes the question before slicing.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Data Analyst (2/5). Revenue per store city in Q1 and in Q2, with the change in % (rounded to 1 decimal), worst change first.
exercises.hint: Pivot with conditional sums: SUM(CASE WHEN d.quarter = 1 THEN f.amount ELSE 0 END). Multiply by 100.0 to avoid integer division.
exercises.answer:
SELECT s.city,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN d.quarter = 1 THEN f.amount ELSE 0 END), 2) AS q1,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN d.quarter = 2 THEN f.amount ELSE 0 END), 2) AS q2,
       ROUND(100.0 * (SUM(CASE WHEN d.quarter = 2 THEN f.amount ELSE 0 END)
                    - SUM(CASE WHEN d.quarter = 1 THEN f.amount ELSE 0 END))
             / SUM(CASE WHEN d.quarter = 1 THEN f.amount ELSE 0 END), 1) AS change_pct
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
JOIN dim_store s ON s.store_key = f.store_key
GROUP BY s.city
ORDER BY change_pct;
exercises.explain: Every store grows (Tunis +13%, Marseille +13%, Paris +35%, Online +56%, Sfax from a small base) except Lyon: 4,762 → 2,630, −44.8%. The total hid it. Conditional aggregation (CASE inside SUM) puts periods side by side in one pass; 100.0 forces a decimal division.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Data Analyst (3/5). Drill down into Lyon: revenue per product category in Q1 and in Q2.
exercises.hint: Same pivot as before, filtered on the Lyon store, grouped by category.
exercises.answer:
SELECT p.category,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN d.quarter = 1 THEN f.amount ELSE 0 END), 2) AS q1,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN d.quarter = 2 THEN f.amount ELSE 0 END), 2) AS q2
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_key = f.product_key
JOIN dim_store s ON s.store_key = f.store_key
WHERE s.city = 'Lyon'
GROUP BY p.category;
exercises.explain: Electronics went from 2,454 to 0, and Accessories (mice, keyboards, hubs, often bought with a laptop) fell from 851 to 354, while Furniture and Office grew. The drop is not the whole store: it is one category, plus the products sold with it.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Data Analyst (4/5). When was the last Electronics sale at Lyon? Return the date (full_date).
exercises.hint: MAX() of the date, filtered on Lyon and the Electronics category.
exercises.answer:
SELECT MAX(d.full_date) AS last_sale
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_key = f.product_key
JOIN dim_store s ON s.store_key = f.store_key
WHERE s.city = 'Lyon' AND p.category = 'Electronics';
exercises.explain: 26 March 2025, and nothing since, in a store that sold electronics every month before. A sudden stop to zero rarely means customers changed their mind: it points to supply (stock-out, delisting, a broken shelf or till setup). The data can say when and where; someone in the store has to say why.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Data Analyst (5/5). Write your answer to the director in 4 to 6 lines: what happened (with the numbers), how sure you are, what to check next and what you recommend.
exercises.hint: Lead with the conclusion, then the evidence, then the next step. Numbers rounded, no SQL.
exercises.answer: Q2 revenue is up 23% (22.0k → 27.1k) and every store grows except Lyon, down 45% (4.8k → 2.6k). The whole drop is Electronics: Lyon has not sold a single electronics item since 26 March (2.5k in Q1, 0 in Q2), and Accessories, usually bought with a laptop, halved; Furniture and Office are up. A drop to zero overnight points to a stock or listing problem rather than demand, but the data cannot prove it. Next: check Lyon's electronics stock and listings since late March with the store manager, and whether Lyon customers switched to the online shop (+56%). Recommendation: fix the supply, then add a weekly store × category alert so a category at zero is caught within days, not a quarter.

exercises.q: Cohorts (practice database shop). Group the customers by the month of their FIRST order: return the cohort month (format YYYY-MM) and the number of customers in it, oldest cohort first.
exercises.hint: A CTE with MIN(ordered_at) per customer_id, then GROUP BY the month. SQLite: strftime('%Y-%m', date).
exercises.answer:
WITH first_orders AS (
  SELECT customer_id, MIN(ordered_at) AS first_at
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', first_at) AS cohort,
       COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM first_orders
GROUP BY cohort
ORDER BY cohort;
exercises.explain: 24 buyers in 5 cohorts: 2025-11: 5, 2025-12: 11, 2026-01: 4, 2026-02: 1, 2026-03: 3. Take MIN() per customer first: grouping orders by month directly counts active customers per month, not cohorts.

exercises.q: Retention (shop). For each first-order cohort (YYYY-MM), count the distinct customers who ordered in the cohort month (m0) and 1, 2 and 3 months later (m1, m2, m3). Return cohort, m0, m1, m2, m3, oldest cohort first.
exercises.hint: Month offset = (year of the order − year of the first order) × 12 + (month − month); in SQLite strftime('%Y', ...) - strftime('%Y', ...) works. Then COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_offset = 1 THEN customer_id END).
exercises.answer:
WITH first_orders AS (
  SELECT customer_id, MIN(ordered_at) AS first_at
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
),
activity AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id,
         strftime('%Y-%m', f.first_at) AS cohort,
         (strftime('%Y', o.ordered_at) - strftime('%Y', f.first_at)) * 12
         + (strftime('%m', o.ordered_at) - strftime('%m', f.first_at)) AS month_offset
  FROM orders o
  JOIN first_orders f ON f.customer_id = o.customer_id
)
SELECT cohort,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_offset = 0 THEN customer_id END) AS m0,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_offset = 1 THEN customer_id END) AS m1,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_offset = 2 THEN customer_id END) AS m2,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_offset = 3 THEN customer_id END) AS m3
FROM activity
GROUP BY cohort
ORDER BY cohort;
exercises.explain: 2025-11: 5, 2, 0, 1; 2025-12: 11, 5, 5, 2; 2026-01: 4, 1, 2, 0; 2026-02: 1, 1, 0, 0; 2026-03: 3, 0, 0, 0. The data stops on 13 March 2026: March is partial, and the zeros of the newest cohorts are offsets not reached yet, which a report should leave empty. December's cohort is the largest and keeps 5 of 11 customers in each of the next two months.

exercises.q: Repeat purchase (shop). Return the number of customers who ordered at least once (buyers), how many ordered at least twice (repeat_buyers) and the repeat-purchase rate in % rounded to 1 decimal.
exercises.hint: Count orders per customer in a CTE, then SUM(CASE WHEN orders >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). Divide by the buyers and multiply by 100.0.
exercises.answer:
WITH per_customer AS (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS buyers,
       SUM(CASE WHEN orders >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS repeat_buyers,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN orders >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS repeat_rate_pct
FROM per_customer;
exercises.explain: 24 buyers, 16 with two orders or more: 66.7%. The denominator is the buyers (24), not the 30 registered customers: 16 / 30 = 53.3% would mix the repeat rate with the signup-to-first-order conversion.

exercises.q: Fix this query (shop): for each signup month (customers.created_at), the number of signups and how many of them ever ordered. The buyers look right, but February 2025 shows 10 signups when only 7 customers signed up that month.
exercises.hint: The LEFT JOIN with orders gives one row per order: what does COUNT(*) count after it?
exercises.answer:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', c.created_at) AS signup_month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) AS signups,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS buyers
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY signup_month
ORDER BY signup_month;
exercises.start:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', c.created_at) AS signup_month,
       COUNT(*) AS signups,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS buyers
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY signup_month
ORDER BY signup_month;
exercises.explain: After the join, a customer with 3 orders is 3 rows, so COUNT(*) counts orders (plus one row per customer without any). COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) counts people: February 2025 has 7 signups and 6 buyers. Customers without an order stay in the result thanks to the LEFT JOIN, and COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) ignores their NULL.

exercises.q: Funnel (shop, table events: user_id, event, at, times in UTC). For March 2026, return the number of distinct users who did view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout and purchase, and the overall conversion view_item → purchase in % rounded to 1 decimal. Some events are logged twice.
exercises.hint: One COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event = '...' THEN user_id END) per step in a single SELECT; filter the month with at >= '2026-03-01' AND at < '2026-04-01'.
exercises.answer:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event = 'view_item' THEN user_id END) AS viewed,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event = 'add_to_cart' THEN user_id END) AS added_to_cart,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event = 'begin_checkout' THEN user_id END) AS began_checkout,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event = 'purchase' THEN user_id END) AS purchased,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event = 'purchase' THEN user_id END)
             / COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event = 'view_item' THEN user_id END), 1) AS conversion_pct
FROM events
WHERE at >= '2026-03-01' AND at < '2026-04-01';
exercises.explain: 40 viewers, 22 added to cart (55.0% of viewers), 13 began checkout (59.1% of carts), 8 purchased (61.5% of checkouts): 20.0% overall. COUNT(*) would count 53 views and 26 add_to_cart events because of repeated events. A half-open range on at keeps the whole last day without BETWEEN's 23:59:59 trick.

interview.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
interview.a: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and is where conditions on COUNT, SUM, etc. go.

INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row of the left table, with NULLs for the right table when there is no match. Use LEFT JOIN when you must not lose rows, for example customers without orders.

All number rows within a window. ROW_NUMBER is always 1, 2, 3 even with ties. RANK gives ties the same number and skips the next ones (1, 1, 3). DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps (1, 1, 2).

interview.q: A query became slow in production. How do you investigate?
interview.a: I reproduce it with EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see the plan and where the time goes, check whether the data volume or the plan changed, and look for full scans, bad row estimates or missing indexes. Then I fix the cause: add or adjust an index, rewrite a non-sargable filter, update statistics or reduce the columns and rows read, and compare the plan before and after.

interview.q: Subquery or CTE: which one do you use and why?
interview.a: They can express the same logic, and modern optimizers such as PostgreSQL 12+ usually inline a CTE used once, so the choice is mostly about readability. I use a subquery for a short, one-off filter and CTEs as soon as the logic has several steps or reuses an intermediate result. For hierarchies I need a recursive CTE, which a subquery cannot do.

interview.q: What happens when a WHERE condition meets a NULL?
interview.a: SQL uses three-valued logic: a comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. So status <> 'cancelled' drops rows where status is NULL, and NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns nothing. I test NULLs explicitly with IS NULL, use COALESCE or IS DISTINCT FROM, and check NULL counts when I profile a table.

They define what a transaction sees of concurrent changes. READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE prevent progressively more anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms. Higher levels are safer but cause more waiting or retries. READ COMMITTED is the default in PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle; under SERIALIZABLE the application must be ready to retry failed transactions.

interview.q: How do you make a data load safe to run twice?
interview.a: I make it idempotent: load into a staging table, deduplicate it, then upsert into the target on its business key with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT or MERGE, or replace a whole partition (delete the day, insert the day) inside one transaction. Rerunning the same load then gives the same result instead of duplicates, which makes retries and backfills safe.

interview.q: How would you build a monthly retention table in SQL?
interview.a: I first fix the definitions: the cohort is the month of the first order (or of signup), and retention in month k means the customer ordered in that month. A CTE gives one row per customer with the cohort month; I join it back to the orders, compute the month offset from the year and month difference, and keep DISTINCT customer, cohort and offset. Then I pivot with COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_offset = k THEN customer_id END) per column and divide by the cohort size. I flag the partial last month and leave offsets not reached yet empty.

interview.q: The checkout conversion in your funnel dropped by half last month. What do you check before raising the alarm?
interview.a: First the data: is the month complete, did tracking change (event renamed, tag missing on a page, consent banner), are events duplicated or deduplicated differently, and are the time zones the same on both sides. Then the definition: distinct users or sessions, open or strict funnel, same date filter. Then I segment by device, browser, country and traffic source to see whether the drop is local, for example one app version, and only then compare with orders in the back office, which is the source of truth for purchases.
